item.title: Google Staff Resign In Backlash Over Its AI Contracts With Military
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from the BBC: Google is facing a backlash from some staff members over the company's deployment of its AI technology for military use. The BBC has spoken to several tech workers who have either recently resigned from Google's AI company, Google DeepMind, or are in the process of leaving, over concerns with the tech firm's military contracts. Sofia Liguori, a London-based research engineer, is one of them. She resigned from Google DeepMind this week and spoke about her concerns exclusively with the BBC, despite her contract restricting her from doing so.
"Realizing my company is pushing more and more for AI systems in military operations makes me feel ashamed to work at Google," Liguori said, speaking in a personal capacity. [...] After working for the company for three years, Liguori said she decided to resign over Google's increasing work with the US and Israeli militaries. "I don't agree with this direction and this has led me to lose faith in my company being true to its stated ethical values," she said. Those values, according to Google's AI Principles, include implementing AI with "human oversight" and aligning the technology with "international law and human rights." But former and current staff at the company, and experts the BBC spoke to, said they were concerned about the level of human oversight at critical moments.
The tech workers said they are particularly worried about the AI military deals signed this year, because they greatly increase the scope of what the Pentagon can use the technology for. Andreas Kirsch, an AI researcher, also resigned from Google DeepMind earlier this month over his concerns. Kirsch told the BBC that he believes "Google's governance and oversight are not sufficient or meaningful enough to deploy AI safely and responsibly in military and classified settings" or "to develop artificial superintelligence safely in the future." "Google seems to have no right to control or veto how the Pentagon uses its AI and also seems to have limited visibility into how it's being deployed," he added.
[...] Employees at Google have told the BBC that staff are scared to speak out about AI safety and its uses in warfare because their employment contracts prohibit them from publicly criticizing the company. "In principle I'm not allowed to criticize Google for the duration of my life," Sofia Liguori told the BBC. But she decided to do so "because I believe it's important for these things to be known and I also think that talking about facts is not criticizing." Liguori added that at Google "people are scared of retaliation and putting their career at risk. You feel you are being watched, you can't speak."
A current employee at Google DeepMind, who declined to be named for fear of retaliation, told the BBC that "a lot of motivated employees who signed up for [the company's] original mission could leave -- but there's also a pipeline of people at the start of the careers who could fill those positions. It could be a changing of the guard." Another Google DeepMind staff member, who also wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC: "A lot of people have left the company that feel strongly about this [how Google DeepMind has changed its ethics position]." "Some people are putting up a fight, others are thinking: 'it's a big company. What do you expect to change?'", the employee said. In response, a Google spokesperson told the BBC: "We work with public sector organisations worldwide and follow a consistent process for reviewing and entering these contracts, including compliance with our acceptable use policies and AI principles."
"We also have dedicated channels for employees to safely raise any concerns -- ranging from business ethics to misconduct -- and have strict workplace policies in place to prevent retaliation of any kind."

item.title: Claude Designed 211 Proteins in Two Days. The Memes-in-Slack Phase Took Two Months
item.author: Penicillin
item.content:encoded: Citrini Research has no lab, no biologists, and no drug discovery experience. It flew to Anthropic's New York office, ran an unreleased Claude against five scorpion toxins, and paid the wet lab on a credit card.The number everyone is quoting from Anthropic's scorpion antivenom post is 318,484 — the count of protein designs an internal Claude model generated in 64 hours before narrowing to 180 for lab testing. It's the wrong number to fixate on.The interesting numbers are 5 and 40. Five is the size of the team that commissioned the work: Citrini Research, a thematic equity research shop that sells investment notes, not medicines. Forty is roughly how many days it took to turn the designs into physical molecules and get data back.A stock research firm walked into a frontier labAnthropic's framing is that it wanted to test whether motivated nonexperts could take a real swing at a human health problem. Citrini approached Anthropic with that question a month before Anthropic published its first protein binder results in August. Nathan C. Frey of Anthropic's team described the result as an entertaining, candid and humbling account of nonexperts — "filthy casuals," in Citrini's self-description — going after a real health problem with Claude.Hunterbrook Media, which embedded with Citrini for the two-day visit, is blunter about what that required. The team didn't do this from a laptop at home. They sat in a conference room on the second floor of Anthropic's NYC office and ran a powerful unreleased model — supervised, but without the bioscience guardrails that demote this kind of work to a less capable model on Anthropic's public tier. Prompts included internal tactics the reporter wasn't permitted to record. The initial prompt itself ran roughly 35 pages.So the headline isn't "nonexperts designed a drug with AI." It's "nonexperts designed a drug with the AI you can't access." Hunterbrook's CEO, a molecular biologist who has co-founded two AI drug design companies, says the gap between Anthropic's public warnings and ordinary users' experience exists because we are not using the same tools.Claude placed the order itselfThe operational detail buried in Anthropic's writeup: at the team's request, Claude emailed the sequences to Twist Bioscience in messages flagged as written by Claude. Twist and Adaptyv Bio synthesized and tested all 211 designs. Per Citrini's own account of the project, the wet lab quoted about $85,000 for the samples, which the firm put on an American Express card, against roughly $200,000 total committed.Set that against how scorpion antivenom is made today. The sole FDA-approved product comes from immunizing horses with milked venom and purifying their antibodies — a method Southern African sting-response expert Jonathan Leeming compared to the moon landing in its era and considers overdue for replacement. The Mexican program behind it took 25 years, then another decade of US trials.Then biology did what biology doesSeventeen of 211 designs met Anthropic's binding criteria. Among the 60 single-toxin designs, 11 were binders — an 18% hit rate Anthropic's own technical report calls consistent with typical protein design campaigns. None of the 151 multitoxin designs bound more than one toxin, which was the ambitious goal and the one that would have mattered most for a cheap universal cocktail.Anthropic does not claim an antivenom. Nothing was tested for neutralization in cells or in animals. Hunterbrook adds that broader testing flagged some binders as potentially sticky, leaving selectivity unconfirmed.The sharpest pushback showed up within hours, in the replies to Citrini's own announcement: proteins that bind scorpion toxins were demonstrated in the literature more than fifteen years ago, and the part that actually matters — neutralization — is exactly the part nobody ran. Naoual Oukkache, who directs an antivenom lab at the Pasteur Institute of Morocco, told Hunterbrook much the same thing in gentler terms: computational design can rationalize several stages of research, but AI-designed molecules are not about to replace polyclonal antivenoms, and are better understood for now as complementary treatments that still need standardized manufacturing and clinical validation.And then the clock. Citrini's own line about it is the best thing written on this entire project: their virtual biologist may have squeezed a year of work into a couple of days, but "biology works at the speed of life." They watched Claude move through problems at a pace that was hard to follow, and then spent the next two months getting acquainted with laboratory turnaround times — an education that, by their account, consisted largely of posting memes in Slack while they waited.Hunterbrook's CEO, who spent a decade in biotech before leaving it, has his own name for that stretch: "the of biotechnology." Contracts, shipping, reagents, subcontractors, emails.Where the bottleneck actually movedCNIO researcher Susana Vázquez Torres, one of two outside experts Anthropic sent the work to, gave the line that reframes the whole thing: designing a binder against almost any target no longer looks unrealistic, and "binding itself is no longer the main bottleneck."The other reviewer, Timothy P. Jenkins of the Technical University of Denmark, framed the same point commercially: hitting five toxins in parallel in a matter of days is the AI-driven shift in therapeutic discovery made legible, and it matters most for diseases like envenomation that have been starved of innovation precisely because nobody could make the economics work.That is a claim about where cost and time now live. If design collapses to a weekend and synthesis-plus-assay becomes the gating step, the scarce resource is wet lab throughput, not computational cleverness. Citrini, being Citrini, turned that into a trade favoring contract research organizations.Everyone with operating experience says the same thing a different way. Transfyr CEO Anna Marie Wagner describes drug development as a funnel that has always been top-heavy: widen the top without widening the middle and you have simply built a tighter bottleneck. Amy Abernethy, formerly a senior FDA leader and now at Insitro, puts the choke point further downstream still — AI is supercharging discovery, but clinical development is a brick wall that arrives sooner or later regardless. And Insitro CEO Daphne Koller pushed back on the premise entirely: making more molecules isn't the hard part. Knowing what to aim them at is, and most failures come from not knowing.The thing worth watching isn't whether Cn2-B1 becomes a drug. It's that the list of people who can credibly start a drug program now includes five analysts with a spreadsheet habit and a corporate card.

item.author: Michael Larabel
item.content:encoded: Linux user-space for several years had shadow stack support for hardware-enforced control-flow enforcement in defending against return oriented programming (ROP) attacks. Intel Tigerlake and newer CPUs or AMD Zen 3 and newer have the necessary hardware shadow stacks support. Shadow stacks have been effective for helping user-space software fend ROP attacks while now there is new work toward bringing shadow stack support for kernel space on Linux...

item.title: Bloom Security Adds Cyera DSPM Context to Rank AI Risk by Data Sensitivity
item.author: Kevin John
item.content:encoded: An alert shows an AI agent on an employee’s laptop opening a connection to a datastore. What should the security team do next? The answer depends heavily on what sits inside that datastore, and that is precisely the information Bloom Security now places beside the event through a new integration with Cyera DSPM.According to information shared directly with this writer, the integration pairs Bloom’s endpoint AI visibility and AI usage control with Cyera’s data sensitivity context. Its purpose is practical: helping security teams understand, prioritize, and enforce policies on AI access to sensitive data.Triage With the Data in ViewBloom, endpoint security purpose-built for the AI-native endpoint, monitors every AI tool and agent running on endpoints. It shows which ones are installed, who is using them, what they connect to, and whether the activity looks risky. For each event, analysts see the agent, the tool, the user, the device, and the connection target.Cyera, the AI Security Platform, fills in the rest. It knows which datastores contain sensitive data such as PII, PHI, PCI, credentials, and business records, along with the volume of each. Attached to a Bloom event, Cyera supplies the sensitivity level, data type, record count, and regulatory classification of the data involved.For a team working through its queue, that pairing shapes how work gets ordered. Activity can be ranked by the sensitivity of the data at stake. During an investigation, responders can see the data impact of an event as part of the same picture, which keeps attention on the events that matter most.Response Options in Real TimeOnce a team spots an agent reaching sensitive data, it has a range of responses available in real time. It can block the activity, pause it, investigate it, or remediate it. The integration provides immediate visibility into which AI agents are accessing which sensitive data, so each of those decisions rests on concrete information.That capability carries weight given how much AI now runs on employee laptops. Employees run dozens of AI agents, MCPs, and tools on their machines, and those tools often connect to cloud datastores, SaaS platforms, and databases where sensitive data lives. Bloom sees the activity. Cyera knows which destinations are sensitive.Policies That Hold EverywhereConsistency is the other operational gain. The integration extends Cyera’s data classification into runtime enforcement at the endpoint, letting teams block AI access to sensitive datastores in real time as agents run.In practice, a team can define a single policy, such as blocking agents from accessing data classified as Sensitive and above. Bloom enforces it on every endpoint, every time. The same standard governs every device in the fleet, with no need to configure each machine separately.For security operations, the intended outcome is that risky AI activity is stopped before sensitive data leaves the organization. Teams that rely on Cyera also gain real-time visibility into endpoint threats to their sensitive data.Bloom’s platform supports this workflow with precise control over every AI tool and the software ecosystem that tool brings with it. Each is assessed against asset intelligence and the full context of the endpoint: who is using it, what else is running, and what data it can reach. Bloom prevents risky installations, fixes misconfigurations, and enforces context-aware runtime policies fleet-wide.Cyera’s platform, built for the age of agents, secures data at rest, in motion, and in use, whether humans or AI agents are touching it. Enterprises including Paramount, Chipotle, and Valvoline use Cyera to control exactly what data their AI can reach and to govern what happens next. As of its June 2026 funding round, Cyera was valued at $12 billion and had raised approximately $2.3 billion, with investors including Accel, Blackstone, Cyberstarts, Georgian, Lightspeed, and Sequoia.Itay Keren, CEO and co-founder of Bloom Security, summed up the thinking behind the integration:“Data security has always been close to my heart, having spent a large part of my career building in this space. The challenge now is that AI agents are running on endpoints with direct access to sensitive data, and traditional endpoint security simply can’t see which agents are touching which data. Bloom monitors endpoint AI activity. Cyera knows what data is sensitive. Together, we’ve brought together endpoint visibility with data context: real-time enforcement grounded in data sensitivity.”This article was published as a press release by the author under HackerNoon's Business Blogging program.

item.title: AEREDIUM Introduces AI Guardrails to Keep Autonomous Agents in Check When Handling Payments and Code
item.author: Ishan Pandey
item.content:encoded: Nine in ten professional developers now use AI coding agents at work every week, according to JetBrains' 2026 survey of more than 15,000 of them. Total stablecoin supply has also grown to about $316 billion, which means a rising share of the software that writes code and sends money runs through agents. AEREDIUM, a digital asset infrastructure company based in Austin, Texas, launched two products on 13 October 2026 for that situation: The Chair, which governs AI coding agents, plus MCP Connector, which governs agents that pay and trade. Both place a policy engine between the agent and the system it wants to touch, so that every proposed action is approved, denied or held for a human to review before anything runs.Stablecoins Give AI Agents Money to MoveStablecoin supply stood at about $27 billion at the end of 2020, reached about $163 billion a year later and finished 2025 near $308 billion, according to DefiLlama figures compiled by Transak, which puts the total at roughly $316 billion on 12 June 2026. Tether's USDT accounts for about 59% of that supply and Circle's USDC for about 24%, while PayPal's PYUSD and the euro-denominated EURC are smaller tokens that sit in the same family of assets. These are the tokens that AEREDIUM's MCP Connector lets an agent send, which connects a market that grew nearly twelvefold in six years with the next group of users who will move it, namely software that acts on a person's behalf.JetBrains found that 90% of professional developers use AI coding agents at work at least weekly and 68% use them daily, based on responses collected between May and July 2026. The mix of tools shifted quickly during the year. Claude Code rose from 18% to 39% of developers since January, Codex went from 3% to 16%. GitHub Copilot slipped from 29% a year earlier to 21%. A tool that executes commands, edits files and pushes changes inside a company's repositories is a new kind of actor inside a software team. The survey shows that most teams already have one working beside them.The Chair sits between an AI agent and an organization's development environment and evaluates each tool call before it runs, covering actions such as executing commands, modifying files, merging code and pushing changes. Requests covered by an existing rule are approved or denied automatically. Requests outside the rules are held in a control panel where authorized users approve or reject them. Every decision produces a signed receipt that documents what the agent attempted, which policy applied and who authorized the action. It supports Claude Code through a dedicated plugin and provides a governed shell for other coding agents including those from OpenAI. Organizations write their policies by answering a questionnaire so they never have to code the rules by hand.Dadon said that AI agents are no longer limited to answering questions, since they write code, move money and make decisions with real consequences. He added that the challenge is making sure they operate within the rules their owners set. He described the two products as a way for organizations to put AI to work without giving up control over what it can do. The Chair is priced at $10 per chair per month or $80 per year after a 30-day free trial. MCP Connector starts at $49 a month across four packages, also with a 30-day trial.MCP Connector Gives Agents Wallets With LimitsMCP Connector applies the same approach to money by combining a policy engine with a digital asset wallet, so that an agent can execute approved payments and trades while staying inside limits its owner has set. Each agent operates through its own wallet, policy and designated owner, who defines the agent's role, approves its mandate with a passkey and can halt or delete the agent at any time.A Payer can send USDC, USDT, PYUSD and EURC to addresses its owner has approved and has no permission to trade, while a Trader can trade on designated exchanges within its own wallet and has no permission to send funds to outside recipients. The wallet uses threshold signatures generated inside secure enclaves, which means no complete private key is ever created and AEREDIUM holds no key to the owner's funds. The product supports Ethereum, Arbitrum and Base, keeps transaction records for seven years and is designed for Claude with openness to OpenAI and other AI frameworks.An Institutional Security Background Behind the ProductsBoth products build on the threshold-signature technology and policy engine that AEREDIUM uses for institutional digital asset security, where a transaction has to satisfy predefined rules before it can be signed and every decision is recorded for later verification. On 2 September 2026 the company launched AERSeal, which uses its AERKey infrastructure to keep key shares in separate hardware-attested enclaves with the CGGMP24 threshold signing protocol so that no full private key exists in one place. Organizations set an M-of-N approval policy that signatories approve with passkeys.The company says it holds United States Patent 12,694,407, granted on 28 July 2026, for a method in which AI models monitor stablecoins to assess whether each coin is backed by the reserves it claims. It operates from Melbourne, Tel Aviv and Austin, Texas.The Outlook for Governing Autonomous AgentsThe market is moving in the direction these products address. Gartner forecasts that 33% of enterprise software applications will include agentic AI by 2028, up from less than 1% in 2024. It also forecasts that 15% of day-to-day work decisions will be made autonomously by then, up from 0%.The same forecast expects more than 40% of agentic AI projects to be canceled by the end of 2027 because of rising costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls. That last item is the one a policy engine with signed receipts is built to answer. AEREDIUM's launch extends its offering from digital asset custody and settlement into the governance of AI-driven financial and software operations. The pricing, the trial periods and the support for several coding agents give teams a low-cost way to test whether rules written in advance can keep pace with the agents they already run on aeredium.ai.Don’t forget to like and share the story!Vested Interest Disclosure: HackerNoon has reviewed the report for quality, but the claims herein belong to the author. #DYOR.

item.title: 333 Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH traffic and retrieve plaintext email
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Unknown hackers hijacked more than 300 Tor exit nodes and reconfigured them to favor unencrypted email traffic and redirect SSH connections through servers they controlled, a researcher reported Tuesday.The hijacking began in late August, when, according to Tor volunteers, the attacker used a valid password that had been reused to gain access to a Tor management server. The attacker then installed Ebury, a backdoor written for Linux that was discovered 12 years ago.Then the attacker connected from the management server to a second Tor server, called Switzerland2, through SSH, using an RSA key that, for unknown reasons, investigators couldn’t find among Switzerland2’s authorized keys. With administrative control of Switzerland2, the attackers installed Ebury there as well. Finally, the attacker reconfigured settings on two exit nodes that Switzerland2 hosted.

item.title: Airbnb Bans Making Guests Do Dishes, Take Out the Trash
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Airbnb is banning hosts from requiring guests to perform time-consuming checkout chores, including washing dishes, stripping beds, doing laundry, and taking trash off-site. The updated policy applies to reservations booked on or after November 20. The Verge reports: Airbnb is displaying hosts' requests more prominently now in a new "rules and requests" section on listings. You might see an "includes cleaning requests" warning if a host leaves chore requests in their listing after the new policy goes into effect. Hosts aren't allowed to sneak in extra rules in messages to guests or on signs around their property, either.
Some hosts pushed back on the house rules restrictions on Airbnb's forums, saying they pose health risks and arguing that guests can simply choose not to stay at listings with overly-strict rules. Airbnb says there can be exceptions to the limits on checkout chores, like asking guests to "dispose of trash in an animal-proof container in bear country."

item.title: How Teams Burn Budgets Testing with Claude and Playwright Without a Harness
item.author: QA.tech
item.content:encoded: In March 2026, Anthropic acknowledged that Claude Code users were hitting usage limits faster than expected. One developer's GitHub report put a five-hour session at 19 minutes. A Hacker News commenter described the fast version: "it launched 102 agents and blew my $120 quota in 6 minutes."Part of that spike traced to Claude Code itself: the same GitHub thread reported two prompt-caching bugs inflating token use by 10 to 20 times, and Anthropic had trimmed session limits at peak hours around the same time. The headline incident was partly a bug. The structural point survives without it. A bug drained one engineer's quota in minutes while he watched. A DIY agentic test suite does the same thing on purpose, unattended, hundreds of times a day. A developer burning a quota is sitting there watching it. A CI job is not.A browser agent's context grows every step: each page snapshot stays in the conversation and is re-read on every following turn.Single-author traces put a Playwright MCP test near 100,000 or more tokens, against roughly 27,000 for a CLI-based loop. Anecdotal, not a controlled study.In one published benchmark, harness choice moved tokens per solved task by up to 70x on the same model.Inference cost per unit of capability falls about 10x a year, and agent workloads inflate consumption faster than that.At 50 to 500 runs a day, none of the above is a rounding error.The token cost of Playwright MCP and ClaudeWhere do the tokens go? Mostly into re-reading.Playwright MCP drives a browser for an LLM by handing back the page as a structured accessibility tree, one at a time. Playwright's own docs put a snapshot at a few hundred tokens for a simple page. Real applications are not simple pages. On a dense dashboard the tree balloons, and every snapshot you take stays resident in the conversation history. Step two re-sends step one's snapshot. Step twelve re-sends all eleven before it. Nothing is de-duplicated.The clearest write-up comes from engineer Kuljeet Singh Shekhawat, who wired Playwright MCP into Claude Code and ran a 15-test sheet. Six tests in, 75% of a 200,000-token context window was gone. In the trace, a single call had consumed 232,000 tokens by itself. His summary of the mechanism: the model is rereading every snapshot, on every turn. Prrammod Dutta's benchmark landed in the same place: by step twelve the conversation carried 90,000 tokens of stale snapshots from screens the agent had already left.Three cost centers, then:Accessibility trees kept in historyRe-read on every subsequent turn (the slow burn)Image payloads for visual stepsLarge and per-step; one call can dwarf a context window (the fast burn)Tool definitions and system prompt loaded at session startRe-sent as part of the conversation floor every single turn (see the harness numbers below)Why cheaper tokens are not a rescueInference cost for a fixed level of capability really is falling fast. Andreessen Horowitz's "LLMflation" analysis puts the drop at roughly 10x a year. The catch is that nobody holds capability fixed. Teams move to the newest frontier model, and frontier is never the cheap one.As investor Ethan Ding argues in AI Subscriptions Get Short Squeezed, the same task that once ran as a single completion now runs a whole agent loop, so consumption climbs even as per-token prices drop; in his words, the math behind flat-rate pricing has broken. From the practitioner side, Sourcegraph's Steve Yegge has pegged heavy agent use at roughly $10 to $12 an hour, which for a working developer lands around $100 to $300 a day. Now stop thinking about a workday and start thinking about a CI schedule that never clocks out.Budgeting on falling token prices assumes constant work per token. Agent testing grows the work per run, unattended.The suite-scale arithmeticThe arithmetic, so you can substitute your own numbers. Illustrative; the methodology note below lists the assumptions.The burn for one full run of a DIY loop is roughly:tokens per step × steps per flow × flows per suite × price per tokenThen multiply by runs per day. Take a modest suite: a blended 8,000 tokens per step (small snapshots plus the growing floor they ride on), 6 steps per flow, 30 flows, at an input price around $3 per million tokens.DIY loop, re-reasons everythingHarness: reason once, replay the restreasoning only on changed pathssmall base plus spikes on real UI changeMethodology: 8,000 tokens per step is a blend of a modest accessibility-tree snapshot and the accumulated floor re-sent each turn; 6 steps per flow and 30 flows describe a small suite; $3 per million is a mid-tier input price in October 2026. Output tokens, retries and screenshots are excluded, so the figure is a floor, not an estimate of your bill.The biggest lever is the scope of what runs, and it is not in the table. A documentation-only change should cost close to nothing. In a naive loop it costs the same as a change to checkout, because nothing classified it first. Risk-weighted scoping cuts more from the bill than any per-token optimization you can do.The model is the cheap part of a harness. The clearest proof comes from an independent benchmark by engineer Eishan Lawrence, surfaced by The New Stack: across 12 harness configurations running an identical model, tokens per solved task ranged from about 3,500 (Aider in architect mode) to about 292,000 (OpenClaw). The suite ran on two unrelated models and the ordering of harnesses barely shifted between them, which is what points at the harness rather than the model. That benchmark measures coding harnesses, not browser-testing harnesses; the mechanism generalizes, the exact numbers are borrowed.The startup tax makes the pattern concrete. The same benchmark reported roughly 700 tokens for Aider in architect mode against roughly 26,000 for OpenClaw, before any real work happens, resent on every turn. A 40x floor paid once would be tolerable. Paid per turn, it is not. That is the "startup tax" row from the cost table above, priced.Why does a naive loop re-reason at all? Because an agent keeps nothing between runs unless something around it does. As QA.tech co-founder and Chief AI Officer Vilhelm von Ehrenheim (fifteen years in machine learning, previously at Klarna) put it in a September talk to the CTO Craft community: an agent forgets everything you told it unless someone has built the memory and context handling around it. That is the one-line reason the same agent tours your application from scratch on run 200 exactly as it did on run 1.Stopping that waste is what a harness does. It models the application once (a crawl builds a persistent map that later runs reuse, instead of rediscovering the UI from scratch), routes complex flows to a heavier agent tier and everything else to a faster one, and confirms results with deterministic checks (network assertions, email and file-download checks, API calls) rather than more token-hungry reasoning. It can also keep the loop inside the tools you already use: through an MCP server, a coding agent like Claude Code starts a run and reads results instead of burning its own context to drive the browser. Past the Bottleneck puts the alternative in one line: an agent that explores from zero every run is slow, inconsistent, and expensive. An agent that starts from zero pays for the guided tour every single time.That changes the shape of the bill, which is easiest to see by pricing model:Suite size × run frequencyA few flows, one owner, no CI schedulePer runner-minute (some AI platforms)Teams that already tune for speedPer test-case execution (QA.tech and some others)Running junk you did not needPredictable CI budgets at scalePer-execution pricing has its own exposure: an entry price is not your cost at a real workload, so ask any vendor (ours included) what a 150-test suite running 100 times a week actually consumes. And if you have a handful of flows, one owner, and no CI schedule, the burn is negligible: build it yourself with Claude plus Playwright, which is fast at scaffolding tests. The curve only bites at suite scale.What actually caps the billRunaway spend is not unique to a DIY loop. Any agentic setup can do it, including a managed one, and anyone who has watched a bill spike knows it. The question is whether the controls exist and whether you had to build them yourself.What you build yourself without itClassifies the change first, so a docs-only pull request triggers almost nothing and a billing change triggers everythingA change classifier and a policy for what each risk level runsLabel-based or on-demand runs, so not every push spends automaticallyTrigger routing in CI, plus a clean way to fall back to on-demand while you tunePer-environment limits on parallel runs, which protect both the bill and the staging serverQueueing and rate limits around your own test infrastructureA persistent model of the app and cached decisions on unchanged pagesStorage, cache invalidation, and a crawl you keep in sync yourselfFailures carry expected versus actual, screenshots, the stack trace, and the API calls that failed, so the agent retries lessA verdict format and all the plumbing to capture itTwo of those deserve a note. Risk scoring is the biggest lever by far: score the change, then decide what to run, and some teams now auto-merge low-risk pull requests on that score because human attention is worth more elsewhere. Actionable evidence is a cost item: a green-or-red result forces manual digging and blind retries, and retries are a line in the cost model above. A verdict an agent can act on directly means fewer full re-runs.Concurrency is also where the DIY loop hits a wall on your own machine. You cannot run ten browsers on the laptop you are trying to work on. Von Ehrenheim's own prediction is that local development fades for exactly this reason: one task in front of one model made local sense, many agents in parallel do not, because you end up bottlenecked serving your own application from your own laptop.You do not need a big regression suiteThe failure mode we watch teams walk into is volume too early: hundreds of unstable tests re-running everything, everywhere, on every push.A calmer shape works better and costs less. Keep a small scheduled regression suite of the flows that must never break, and run dynamic testing on every pull request where the diff decides what actually runs. Chasing 100% coverage works against you here: more surface to re-run for less signal.Not everything needs a model, either. As von Ehrenheim puts it: don't bring a huge hammer to a small nail. Some checks are invariants, things that should never change and can be codified cheaply: an architectural rule about which modules may import which, a contract that blocks a merge on a breaking API change, a constraint that keeps personal data out of the logs. A linter is the simplest invariant. They run on every change for almost nothing. Judges, a model reading the result, are for what is too fluid to codify. Run a model over everything and you pay frontier prices for work a codified check does for free.If you would rather not build itMaintaining the loop, the world model, and the token budget yourself is real work, and it drifts out of alignment every time the UI moves. That is what a managed agentic testing platform like QA.tech is for: it does the amortization as a product and ships the controls above. It will not make a runaway impossible, nothing does; it makes the caps someone else's code. If your CI is already competing with your engineers for tokens, a short demo is the fastest way to see whether the shape fits.The same loop that drained one engineer's quota in minutes is what a DIY suite runs hundreds of times a day, and a nightly job notices at the end of the month. Your CI should not be competing with your engineers for tokens.How many tokens does an AI browser test use? There is no fixed number, but anecdotal single-author traces put a Playwright MCP loop near 100,000 or more tokens per test, driven mostly by accumulated page snapshots.Why does Playwright MCP use so many tokens? Because each page snapshot stays in the conversation and is re-read on every following turn, so context and cost grow with every step you take.Is per-token or per-execution pricing better for testing? Per-execution pricing makes a CI budget predictable because cost tracks tests run rather than tokens consumed, though you should still ask what a real workload actually costs.Do cheaper models fix agent testing costs? No, because agent workloads inflate token consumption faster than per-token prices fall, and teams keep moving to the newest frontier model.How do you keep agentic testing costs down? Scope runs by risk, cap concurrency, reuse a persistent model of the app, and reserve the model for what cannot be checked with a cheap deterministic assertion.

item.title: Check Point’s New AI Firewall Reflects Changes in How Enterprises Approach AI Security
item.author: Ishan Pandey
item.content:encoded: Check Point's new solution is the latest sign that AI security is being absorbed into infrastructure enterprises already trust, rather than treated as a separate system to adopt.Enterprises are deploying artificial intelligence faster than security teams can secure it with an AI-specialized cyber tech stack. Evaluating, purchasing, and deploying a new security system takes time, and few organizations are willing to slow their AI rollout to wait for that process to finish.Security vendors are responding by extending the platforms already running in production, rather than trying to sell enterprises something new. Released in late July, Check Point’s AI Network Firewall is the latest, clearest example of this shift.These days, there’s quite a bit of confusion about what an AI firewall is. That confusion is itself a sign of how early we still are in the lifecycle of this category. Traditional network firewall providers are bolting on AI features to help those systems better protect corporate networks from evolving cyber threats. But they’re still legacy security systems. On the other hand, there is an entirely new breed of AI firewall that’s specifically designed to protect AI models and applications. That’s the category Check Point’s AI Network Firewall belongs to.How Check Point’s AI Network Firewall protects AI applications at the network layerCheck Point is among the vendors leading a deeply integrated approach to protecting AI environments. With its new AI Network Firewall, it’s able to address the three core attack surfaces enterprises are most concerned about.The first is their employees. It has become common to use both sanctioned and unsanctioned AI tools on a daily basis to get work done faster. This is great for productivity, but from a security perspective it’s alarming, because existing data protection tools were never designed to work with AI models.Check Point’s firewall protects against employee AI use by first discovering which AI apps and tools employees are actually using, sanctioned and shadow alike, then applying intent-based classification to their prompts. This allows it to understand the context of what people are asking AI to do, so the firewall can prevent them from feeding sensitive information to third-party models. This kind of visibility gap is exactly what’s driving CISOs to build formal audit frameworks for shadow AI risk in the first place.Autonomous AI agents and MCP traffic are the second major attack surface. Employees aren’t just asking AI to answer questions anymore. These days, they’re having AI do the actual work too. But these agents need to be carefully governed to prevent them from doing something disastrous, such as deleting a critical database. Check Point counters this risk by discovering all of the AI agents and MCP servers operating in an enterprise’s environment, then enforcing policy on that traffic in real time, blocking an agent from accessing a resource or taking an action the moment it falls outside what’s allowed.Finally, there are the AI applications and models themselves. Check Point protects these with a defensive inline prompt injection system, built based on tech developed by Lakera, the AI security startup that Check Point acquired to bring purpose-built prompt-injection defense into its platform. The firewall blocks adversarial inputs and data exfiltration attempts before they reach the underlying model, and it screens the model’s own outputs for harmful or manipulated responses before they reach the end user.These capabilities are deployed directly into the firewalls Check Point’s customers are already running. There’s no need to purchase any new hardware or software, and no new console to contend with. Customers just update their existing infrastructure, and they’re good to go.Many of Check Point’s peers have taken the same approach, extending their existing firewalls rather than building something new. A prime example is Zscaler, which debuted AI Broker, Endpoint AI Security and AI Access Graph features within its flagship Zero Trust Exchange platform in June, as opposed to launching a new product.Not every vendor is taking that route, though. Cloudflare has gone in the opposite direction with its dedicated AI Gateway product, a standalone service that adds guardrails, rate limiting, and traffic controls in front of AI application calls rather than folding that protection into infrastructure customers already run.There are arguments for both approaches. Some teams may benefit from the distinction between traditional and AI cyber defenses. For others, it makes sense to avoid dealing with yet another dashboard, especially if they’re already contending with security tool fragmentation.“Organizations are challenged to deploy dedicated AI security solutions, which are additive to their existing security architecture, contributing to the sprawl of dis-jointed, siloed security tools and agents,” says Pete Finalle, Research Manager of Trusted Access and Network Security at International Data Corp. “While rare, the native integration of AI security across existing enforcement points provides improvements to visibility, telemetry effectiveness, security posture and management simplicity.”In the case of Check Point, the AI Network Firewall lives under the umbrella of its AI Defense Plane, as part of a unified security and governance system that spans AI applications, APIs, browser plugins, cloud environments and endpoints. The AI Network Firewall is one of several enforcement points, alongside endpoint agents and browser plugins, through which the AI Defense Plane’s policy gets applied at the network layer.The cost of waiting, according to breach dataSecuring AI has become a matter of urgency. In a recent study, IBM found that shadow AI incidents hit 43% of breached organizations, up from 20% the year before. This illustrates why enterprises are so nervous about their employees’ use of AI tools. In many cases, staff simply ignore corporate policy and start feeding data to their favored AI chatbots, but doing so can be extremely costly, as the IBM report puts the average cost of a shadow AI security breach at a staggering $5.39 million.IBM’s study also revealed that breaches involving an organization’s own models or apps rose from 13% to 21% in the last year, which explains why security teams have every reason to be concerned about the AI application and model layer, too.The numbers are alarming, and they explain why security vendors prefer to expand their existing tools instead of taking the time to build something entirely new. By extending existing infrastructure, they can offer new AI protections much faster than if they were to create an entirely new platform.These add-ons are easier for organizations to deploy, too, since in most cases the path is a version upgrade to infrastructure they already run, not a new system to install, configure and learn from scratch. Compare that to installing an entirely new AI network gateway, which could take weeks or even months to properly integrate and learn. Most businesses would rather close the AI exposure gap right now if given the chance.Why analysts can’t agree on the size of this marketAnalysts don’t share a definition for the AI firewall category itself, and that lack of consensus is why their size estimates vary so widely. Some lump it in with traditional network firewalls that have simply added AI features. Others count only the newer category of firewalls built specifically to defend AI itself.According to IT-Harvest, the market for LLM firewalls and protection tools was worth around $30 million last year, though its revenue is projected to double by the end of 2026. The organization came up with that modest number because its study focused on that specific segment of AI firewalls only, as opposed to the broader AI security segment. It’s a much lower figure than 360iResearch’s projected $260 million valuation of the AI firewall market for 2026.The problem is that security vendors don’t really agree on exactly what an AI firewall is. Some prefer to use the term “LLM firewall,” while others dump them in the “AI model protection” category, explains IT-Harvest analyst Richard Stiennon in a recent interview.This confusion is consistent with the architectural shift of some security vendors. When AI security is bundled as part of a broader platform that enterprises are already paying for, such as with Check Point’s or Zscaler’s platforms, spending on those tools will be bundled into whatever existing category they fall into. That makes it much harder to narrow down the true size of demand for AI firewalls and other AI security solutions.The confusion only deepens once you account for two more trends in the “AI security” space. Scores of cybersecurity tools now use AI internally to power their own detection capabilities and user interfaces, while another wave of vendors are updating existing products specifically to defend against AI-generated attacks.Beyond the naming problemUntil the security industry settles on a universal definition for the technology that protects AI, separate from tools that merely use AI or defend against AI-driven threats, it will struggle to value this market accurately. What’s more, this lack of consensus around terminology makes it harder for enterprises to select the right tools to protect their environments.Nonetheless, enterprises can be reassured that, regardless of labels, the important thing is that security vendors are striving to close the vulnerability gap that the rapid uptake of AI has created. The industry is moving away from isolated solutions, with AI security instead being absorbed into the legacy infrastructure that enterprises already use and trust. Check Point’s AI Network Firewall is one of the clearest signs of where that shift is heading, whatever the ecosystem ends up calling it.Don’t forget to like and share the story!Vested Interest Disclosure: HackerNoon has reviewed the report for quality, but the claims herein belong to the author. #DYOR.

item.title: Flare Lets XRP Holders Borrow Without Selling as Nearly 90% of FXRP Goes to Work in DeFi
item.author: Ishan Pandey
item.content:encoded: FXRP is the token that Flare's FAssets system issues against XRP. It went live on Flare mainnet on 24 September 2025 so that XRP holders could use their holdings in lending, borrowing, staking and trading. The XRP asset base is large, with about 63 billion XRP in circulation worth close to $96 billion at the prices used in the report, while the roughly 145 million FXRP in circulation represent about 0.23% of that supply. At that level of penetration every additional 1% of circulating XRP that moves into FXRP would amount to about 630 million tokens, which is more than four times the current FXRP supply and shows how much room the product has to grow from a very small base.FXRP Supply Growth Since the September 2025 LaunchDemand arrived at once, since the first-week cap of 5 million FXRP filled in about four hours after launch. The supply then passed 90 million by the end of January 2026 and reached 155 million by late April. About 145 million FXRP were in circulation in late September, according to the DefiLlama report, which does not explain the change from the April peak. The report also notes that Flare's incentive program allocated 2.2 billion FLR between July 2025 and July 2026, so the supply built up during a period of active rewards and has held above 140 million since.Where Deployed FXRP Works Across DeFiLending markets hold the largest share of the deployed FXRP at about 52%, spread across Morpho and Kinetic on Flare, Morpho on Ethereum and Euler on Monad. Firelight staking holding 39% and DEX liquidity and smaller venues the remaining 8%, according to the report. Deployment peaked at about 142 million FXRP in May 2026 and measured 136 million on 9 July and 129 million in October, a decline of about 5% since the incentive program ended. That makes the 129 million figure a number that holders have kept in place without the earlier rewards, which is a useful signal for a product that is only a year old.Most of the lending demand comes from holders who use FXRP as collateral and borrow against it while keeping their XRP. In the Sentora RLUSD vault on Morpho on Ethereum, 10.6 million FXRP backed $7.9 million of RLUSD supplied in late September. At the XRP price implied by the report's own figures of about $1.52 that works out to roughly $16 million of collateral behind $7.9 million of borrowing, an implied loan-to-value of about 49% by our estimate, which shows holders borrowing well inside the value of what they post.Cross-Chain Adoption Across Seven NetworksAbout 20 million FXRP are now deployed outside Flare, up from about 4 million on 9 July, a fivefold increase that the report ties to FXRP's issuance as a LayerZero OFT. FXRP now reaches seven networks, namely Ethereum, Base, BNB Chain, Monad, Katana, HyperEVM and HyperCore. It became the first XRP spot pair on HyperCore in January 2026. The amount deployed on Flare itself fell from 132 million to 109 million over the same period, so the off-Flare balance is taking a growing share of a supply that is staying inside DeFi.The Data Layer Behind Flare's RevenueThe DefiLlama report spends as much time on Flare's data infrastructure as on XRP. The numbers explain why. Since FIP.16 took effect, fees from the Flare Data Connector, which verifies events on other chains, have grown faster than any other protocol revenue source and now account for 45% of the total, with protocol revenue running at about $190,000 a month since September, or about $2.3 million annualized. Flare's price feeds come from about 100 staked validators, with block-latency feeds updating roughly every 1.1 seconds. The network cut FLR inflation to 3% from 14 May 2026 under FIP.16, which passed in April with 98.06% of the vote and lowered the issuance cap from 5 billion to 3 billion FLR. The full report describes these changes as a shift toward revenue that comes from using the network.Staking After the July Hard ForkA hard fork on 14 July weighted P-chain stake five times as heavily as delegation for vote power. The share of staked FLR held through direct staking rose from about 32% to 46% of all staked or delegated FLR between April and August, according to the report. About 47 billion FLR, roughly half of circulating supply, is now staked or delegated. About 22.6 billion FLR sits in direct staking. Base gas fees rose from 25 to 500 gwei at the same time, lifting the average fee per transaction from about 0.05 FLR to about 0.21 FLR, which gives the network a steadier fee stream next to the data fees.The next phase centers on Flare Confidential Compute, which lets smart contracts verify results derived from private institutional data without exposing the data itself. Its first institutional application is live on Songbird, Flare's canary network, after governance approval in July 2026, where it supports proof of reserves for Hex Trust's USDX stablecoin. DefiLlama writes that as applications expand, Confidential Compute moves closer to an oracle primitive for private data, which would give institutional information the role that the FTSO price oracle plays for public prices.The report names three milestones that will help decide whether Flare can take its data infrastructure beyond XRP: Bitcoin integration through the planned FBTC product, mainnet deployment of Confidential Compute and growth in protocol revenue. Each one builds on a foundation that is already visible in the numbers, with nearly 90% of FXRP supply in use, cross-chain deployment up fivefold in three months and a data fee line that supplies nearly half of revenue, which gives institutions a working record to evaluate on Flare as the next products arrive.Don’t forget to like and share the story!

item.title: America's War Department Will Test Heat Ray Weapon For Potential Use
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded: Longtime Slashdot reader destinyland shares a report from CNN: The Pentagon has given the Department of Homeland Security permission to test a military-grade heat ray and develop tactics to potentially use it in operations at the southern US border, according to a memo signed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last month and obtained by CNN. The heat ray, officially known as the Active Denial System, is a nonlethal weapon that shoots an invisible beam of electromagnetic waves that can reach a little more than half a mile away, according to the US military. The energy beam causes a burning sensation when it comes into contact with the human skin -- which Pentagon officials have previously compared to feeling a blast of heat when opening a hot oven. Military officials have said the resulting "tingling effect" lasts between 10 and 15 minutes but also generates "an instinctive and irresistible urge to run from the effect."

item.title: Startup Claims To Use AI-Created Viruses To Treat a Patient
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: For the first time, scientists say they have used viruses designed by artificial intelligence to treat a human patient. Researchers announced on Tuesday that they had administered the virus, known as a phage, to a patient suffering from a deadly bacterial infection. Phages attack bacteria, and the hope is that this one will kill the microbes causing the infection. Radical Numerics, the start-up that created the viruses, posted a technical report about them on its website. But the company declined to provide information about the patient or the doctors running the trial, citing confidentiality requirements.
[...] In 2025, researchers at the Arc Institute in Palo Alto, Calif., created an A.I. model called Evo 2, which they trained on millions of DNA sequences, including phage genes. They prompted Evo 2 to make new genomes similar to those in a group of phage species. The A.I. generated 700,000 virus genomes. The team synthesized DNA molecules from 285 genomes and inserted them into bacteria. The researchers found that 16 of the genomes gave rise to viable viruses. Three members of the Evo team, including Dr. Nguyen, left to found Radical Numerics. In June, the company unveiled a new A.I. model, called Omnii, based on some of the same principles as Evo.
Omnii can be trained not just on DNA but also on other aspects of biology, such as the structures of proteins and molecules that keep genes turned on or off. The company is now using Omnii to tackle a range of challenges, including designing cancer vaccines and recognizing the risk that a virus may cause a pandemic. Among these efforts is the first trial of A.I.-designed phage therapy. The researchers created variations of a phage called T7. The virus, which only infects E. coli, looks like a microscopic Apollo lunar lander: a ball-shaped protein shell that holds its DNA atop six leglike protrusions. To infect a bacterium, T7 lands on its surface, using its legs to anchor in place. It then injects its DNA into the cell.
Omnii generated new viral genes altering the shapes of T7's legs, according to Dr. Nguyen and his colleagues. While some of the new legs were significantly different from natural ones, Omnii's phages could still infect bacteria. Once the researchers were confident their strategy had worked, they partnered with doctors treating a patient with a stubborn E. coli infection. The bacteria had resisted not just antibiotics but all the available phages. The researchers said they had trained Omnii with information about the resistant strain and told it to design T7 phages with legs that could grab onto the bacteria. Once the A.I. generated genomes for new viruses, the scientists said they produced the corresponding DNA molecules and inserted them in bacteria. The bacteria became infected and produced T7 phages that could successfully infect, and kill, other microbes. After running tests to make sure the phages were safe, Radical Numerics presented them to the doctors. The F.D.A. authorized a trial. While the trial was authorized by the FDA, it's worth noting that the research has not yet been peer-reviewed in a scientific journal and there's no guarantee the AI-designed phages will work.
However, if it does prove successful, it could help speed phage therapy by cutting down the time it takes to create a new virus tailored to each patient's infection. "We think we can get it done in days," said Dr. Eric Nguyen, the chief executive officer of Radical Numerics.
